VPAT / ACCESSIBILITY CONFORMANCE REPORT GENERATOR

Turn your own WCAG 2.1 self-assessment into a VPAT-shaped ACR.

Fill in the conformance level and remarks for each of the 50 WCAG 2.1 Level A/AA success criteria yourself -- this tool never tests your product or picks a level for you. It formats your answers into the standard document reviewers expect, flags rows a reviewer would reject as incomplete, and lets you export or print the result. Nothing you type leaves this browser. Need the axe-core scan that feeds your own testing formatted into a dated evidence record instead of a procurement ACR? See the Shopify storefront evidence report or the ADA Title II government-site evidence report -- both take the same kind of automated-test output this generator's remarks should be grounded in.

Why did procurement reject our VPAT? — what a reviewer checks first, and the three header fields and blank remarks that get a report sent back.

This generator vs. hiring a paid VPAT/ACR consultant — what a $2,000-5,000 engagement includes that this free tool does not, and does.

This generator vs. filling out the VPAT template by hand — the completeness gaps typing into the official template doesn't catch.

1. Report header

* Flagged as a completeness issue below if left blank.

2. Criteria (WCAG 2.1 Level A and AA)

Choose the conformance level you have determined for each criterion through your own testing. Remarks are required whenever you choose Partially Supports or Does Not Support -- that is the one thing this tool checks for you.

CriterionConformance levelRemarks and explanations

3. Generate


Fill in the form above and choose Generate ACR.

Common questions

Does this tool test my product for accessibility, or fill in the conformance levels for me?

No. You choose every conformance level and write every remark yourself, based on your own testing. This tool only formats your answers into the standard VPAT/ACR table -- it does not scan, crawl, or assess your product, and it never decides a conformance level on your behalf.

What is a VPAT and what is an ACR?

VPAT (Voluntary Product Accessibility Template) is a standardized template published by the Information Technology Industry Council (ITI) for documenting how a product conforms to accessibility standards such as WCAG. A completed VPAT is called an Accessibility Conformance Report (ACR). U.S. federal agencies require one under Section 508, and many state, university, and enterprise procurement processes now ask for one too.

Which standard does this generator cover?

WCAG 2.1 Level A and Level AA -- the 50 success criteria most current ACRs are scored against. It does not cover WCAG Level AAA or the WCAG 2.2 additions.

Is my draft uploaded anywhere?

No. Everything you type stays in this browser tab. A draft auto-save to your browser's own localStorage is optional and can be turned off; nothing is ever sent to a server.

Is VPAT a trademark?

Yes. VPAT® is a registered trademark of the Information Technology Industry Council (ITI). This tool is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by ITI; the name is used only to describe the document format this tool generates.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal, compliance, or accessibility-audit advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional or your own testing. This tool does not test, assess, or audit your product, and it does not determine any criterion's conformance level -- every level and remark above is yours to enter, based on your own testing, and you remain solely responsible for the accuracy of everything you submit. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for meeting any obligation it helps you prepare for. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. This tool is free and experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use it as a system of record; if you need it to survive, export your inputs and run it yourself.

Local-only privacy: everything you type is never uploaded. We count only anonymous feature events in localStorage, with an opt-out. License

Free and open source. If this saved you a trip to a paid VPAT template, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-filling-out-the-vpat-template-by-hand.text:
← VPAT / Accessibility Conformance Report Generator

This generator vs. filling out the VPAT template by hand

The official Word or Excel VPAT template already has the right table shape. It has no way to check the 50 rows you type into it — which is where a completeness gap a reviewer rejects the report over actually comes from.

What filling out the template by hand involves

ITI publishes the VPAT 2.5 template as a Word or Excel document. Using it means downloading it, then typing a conformance level (Supports, Partially Supports, Does Not Support, Not Applicable, or Not Evaluated) and a Remarks cell for each of the 50 WCAG 2.1 Level A and AA success criteria, grouped under the standard's four principles, plus a handful of header fields — product name, version, report date, vendor contact, and evaluation methods used.

The template gets the shape right by construction: the rows, the criterion IDs, and the column headers are already there. What it cannot do is notice anything about what you type into it. A blank Remarks cell next to “Partially Supports” is, to the template, indistinguishable from a filled one — both are just a cell in a table.

What you're trying to get rightTyping into the official templateThis generator
All 50 WCAG 2.1 A/AA criterion IDs and names are present and spelled correctly.Copied or typed by hand from the standard; a transposed digit or a re-copied row from a prior ACR is easy to miss across 50 rows.Pre-populated from the standard's own criterion list. You never type an ID or a name.
Every Partially Supports or Does Not Support row explains why in Remarks.No prompt or check. A blank Remarks cell types in exactly like a filled one.Flagged automatically: any row at either level with an empty Remarks field is listed as a completeness issue before you're done.
The required header fields — product name, report date, evaluation methods used — are actually filled in.Easy to leave one blank while focused on the 50-row table, with nothing calling it out.Checked the same way as the row-level issues, in the same pass.
Seeing how many issues remain before you submit, not after a reviewer sends it back.Requires a manual second read-through of the whole document to catch what typing it once didn't.A running list of every remaining issue, updated as you fill in the form.
Starting the next product's ACR from a clean, correctly-shaped document instead of last time's edited copy.Many vendors duplicate a previous VPAT and edit it, which can carry over a stale row untouched.One fill-in, a fresh, correctly-shaped document every time.

Typing directly into the official template is not wrong — it is the same document shape either way, and every conformance level and remark still comes from your own testing. What the template does not do is check what you typed, which is the specific gap this generator closes.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, formatting runs in your browser, and nothing you type is uploaded anywhere.

Five gaps in one worked example

Score 50 criteria as 42 Supports, 5 Partially Supports, 2 Does Not Support, and 1 Not Applicable — a plausible result for a mostly conformant product with a few known gaps. Write Remarks on two of the five Partially Supports rows and one of the two Does Not Support rows, and leave the rest blank, the way a long form gets filled in under a deadline. Leave the Report Date header field blank too.

Typed straight into the official template, that document looks finished: every row has a level, the table is the right shape, and nothing marks it incomplete. This generator, given the same answers, lists 5 completeness issues — the three unexplained Partially Supports rows, the one unexplained Does Not Support row, and the blank Report Date — before you export anything.

Common questions

Isn't the official VPAT template just a form I fill in?

Yes, and for the format alone that's enough: the ITI-published Word or Excel template already has the right table shape. What it does not do is check your own answers as you type them. Across 50 WCAG 2.1 A/AA rows, a Partially Supports or Does Not Support entry with no Remarks, or a blank header field like Evaluation Methods Used, types in without any warning -- the template accepts an incomplete row exactly as readily as a complete one.

How often does a hand-typed VPAT end up with a row like that?

Easily. In a worked example with 50 criteria scored 42 Supports, 5 Partially Supports, 2 Does Not Support, and 1 Not Applicable, three of the five Partially Supports rows and one of the two Does Not Support rows were typed with no Remarks, and the Report Date header field was left blank -- five completeness gaps in one document, none of which the template itself flagged, because a blank cell and a cell with one word both look like "done" while typing.

Why does an unexplained Partially Supports row matter so much?

Because WebAIM's own published procurement guidance names it as the specific pattern reviewers distrust: a partial or non-conforming criterion with no explanation reads as untested or hidden rather than honestly assessed, and it is the detail a reviewer checks first. A hand-typed document has no mechanism to catch its own gap before submission -- only a second, careful read-through does, and that read-through is exactly the step a deadline tends to compress.

Does this generator decide the conformance levels for me instead?

No. Every level and every remark still comes from your own testing, typed in by you, the same as filling in the official template by hand. The only difference is what happens after you type: this tool assembles the same 50 criterion IDs and names correctly by construction, and checks the result against the two completeness rules above before you submit it -- it does not test, scan, or assess your product, and it never chooses a conformance level on your behalf.

Open the VPAT / Accessibility Conformance Report Generator, or read why procurement rejects a VPAT.

No warranty. This free tool is informational only. It is not legal, compliance, or accessibility-audit advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional or your own testing. It does not test, assess, or audit your product, and it does not determine any criterion's conformance level. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. Everything you type stays on this device. VPAT® is a registered trademark of the Information Technology Industry Council (ITI); this page is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by ITI. It names no competing product or company — it describes only the manual habit of typing into ITI's own published template.

Free and open source. If it helps you ship an ACR, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-hiring-a-vpat-consultant.html.text:
← VPAT / Accessibility Conformance Report Generator

This generator vs. hiring a paid VPAT/ACR consultant

A paid consulting engagement usually bundles two things: testing your product, then formatting the result into the standard table. This free tool only does the second half — it turns conformance answers you already have into a correctly formatted ACR, and catches the completeness gaps that get a report sent back.

What each one is for

A paid VPAT/ACR consulting engagement — the kind offered by accessibility consultancies, typically priced around $2,000-$5,000 per public pricing pages in this space — usually includes manual and automated testing of your product against WCAG, a consultant's own judgment on each criterion's conformance level, and the finished document assembled from that testing.

This generator only assembles. You (or your own engineering, QA, or accessibility team) choose every conformance level and write every remark from your own testing; the tool formats those answers into the standard VPAT 2.5-shaped table and flags the specific completeness problems that make an ACR look untrustworthy to a procurement reviewer — an unexplained partial-support row, or a missing header field. See why procurement rejects a VPAT for the reviewer's own checklist this is built against.

It exists because the two halves have very different costs. Testing requires accessibility expertise or tooling your team may or may not have yet; formatting a 50-row table correctly, consistently, and completely does not, and there is no reason to pay a consultant's rate for the part a deterministic tool does for free.

Have we already tested our product's WCAG conformance?Not this tool's question — that testing has to happen first, by you or a consultant.
We know our conformance levels; how do we format an ACR?This generator — free, in your browser, no account.
Will our draft look complete to a procurement reviewer?This generator's completeness check, before you submit.
Should we pay for a full accessibility audit instead?A different, larger decision this tool does not evaluate.
Is our draft uploaded anywhere?No. Everything stays in this browser tab; optional local-only autosave never leaves your device.

This generator is a formatting tool, not an audit or testing service. It does not test, scan, or assess your product, and it does not determine any criterion's conformance level on your behalf.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, formatting runs in your browser, and nothing you type is uploaded anywhere.

Common questions

Should I use this generator or hire a paid VPAT/ACR consultant?

Depends what you still need. A paid consulting engagement typically bundles two separate things: testing your product against WCAG (manual, automated, or both) to determine each criterion's conformance level, and formatting the results into the standard ACR table. This tool only does the second half. If you or your engineering/QA team have already tested the product and know your conformance levels, this tool gets you a correctly formatted ACR for free. If nobody has tested the product yet, no formatting tool — this one included — can substitute for that testing.

Does this tool test my product for accessibility conformance the way a consultant would?

No, and it is built specifically not to. You choose every conformance level (Supports, Partially Supports, Does Not Support, Not Applicable) and write every remark yourself, from your own testing. The tool never scans, crawls, or assesses your product, and it never determines a conformance level on your behalf — that keeps the liability where it belongs: every substantive claim in the finished report is yours, based on your own testing, not an automated guess this tool made.

What does the completeness check catch that a consultant would also flag?

The specific pattern WebAIM's own guidance on VPAT procurement names as the recurring problem: a Partially Supports or Does Not Support row with no remark explaining why, and a missing header field. A reviewer treats an unexplained partial-support row as untrustworthy regardless of who assembled the document, so this tool flags exactly that gap before you submit — the same completeness bar a consultant reviewing a draft would apply.

Why would a small vendor use this instead of paying for a consultant?

Cost and completeness, not quality of testing. A $2,000-5,000 engagement prices some vendors out of documenting conformance at all, which means a buyer gets no ACR rather than a partial one. A vendor that has already done some of its own testing — even informally, even incomplete — can use this tool to produce a properly formatted, honestly partial ACR today, rather than skip the requirement entirely while saving for a consultant.

why-procurement-rejects-a-vpat.html.text:
SECTION 508 AND ENTERPRISE PROCUREMENT

Why did procurement reject our VPAT?

Almost never because the product failed a criterion. Reviewers expect gaps — every real product has them, and an ACR claiming full conformance across all fifty criteria is the one that draws suspicion. Documents get sent back because they cannot be read as evidence: a row marked as a partial failure with nothing written beside it, a missing date, no statement of how any of it was tested. The reviewer is not judging your product. They are judging whether your document lets them judge your product.

Open the free VPAT/ACR generator

The reviewer's actual problem

Put yourself on the other side of the table. Someone has three ACRs from three vendors and a deadline. They cannot install your software, they cannot run a screen reader against it, and they are not going to take your word for anything they cannot see stated. Every conclusion they reach comes out of the document in front of them.

That makes an empty Remarks cell the most expensive thing in the file. A criterion marked Partially Supports has told the reviewer that something is broken. With nothing beside it, they have no way to tell a cosmetic focus-outline gap from a form nobody using a screen reader can complete — so the defensible assumption is the second one. The row you left blank to avoid drawing attention is the row that gets read most harshly.

What a usable remark looks like

Sent back: “Partially Supports. Some issues exist.”

Accepted: “Partially Supports. The data-grid column headers are not programmatically associated with their cells, so NVDA and JAWS announce cell values without the column name. Affects the reporting module only; the same data is available in the CSV export, which is fully accessible. Fix scheduled for the 4.2 release.”

An illustration of the shape, not a template to copy — the content has to come from your own testing of your own product. What makes the second version work is that it names the component, the assistive technology, the user-facing consequence, and whether there is a way around it.

WebAIM's own procurement guidance singles out generic remarks as a distinct failure from missing ones, and the reason is worth sitting with: “partially conformant” pasted onto twelve rows tells a reviewer those rows were filled in rather than evaluated. It reads as less trustworthy than a blank, because a blank at least does not pretend.

The three header fields that decide whether the rest gets read

A conformance table with no context is not evidence of anything. Three fields carry most of that context, and a report missing them is hard to weigh against a competitor's:

Product name and version. An ACR describes a specific build. Without the version, a reviewer cannot tell whether it covers what they are about to buy.

Report date. Distinguishes a current assessment from one written three releases ago and never revisited. An undated ACR is treated as old.

Evaluation methods used. The single field that separates a tested report from an asserted one. Say what you actually did: which assistive technologies and versions, which browsers, manual testing or automated scanning or both, and who performed it.

The generator on this site will not let those three go quietly. It lists each blank one alongside the row-level problems, before you export, while it is still cheap to fix.

Not Evaluated is a real answer

The template carries five values, and Not Evaluated is one of them. It is the honest label for a criterion nobody has tested yet, and it is a far better position than a guess. A guess that proves wrong is a misrepresentation in a document attached to a bid, with consequences that outlast the bid; an admitted gap is a scheduling conversation. A reviewer who sees three Not Evaluated rows and a note about when they will be covered is looking at an ACR written by someone who genuinely evaluated the other forty-seven.

Unanswered criteria default to Not Evaluated here rather than being dropped from the document, for the same reason: a fifty-row table with forty-one rows in it raises a question the vendor did not mean to raise.

What this tool does, and the line it will not cross

It formats your answers and checks them for completeness. It does not scan your product, does not crawl anything, and never picks a conformance level for you — every value and every remark is yours, entered from your own testing, and you remain responsible for all of it. That boundary is the whole design: a tool that guessed at conformance levels would be producing an assessment it is in no position to make, in a document you are signing.

What it can do is make sure the document you sign does not fail for a reason that has nothing to do with your product.

Common questions

Why would a reviewer reject a VPAT when our product conforms well?

Because conformance and evidence are different things. A reviewer cannot verify your product; they can only read your document. An ACR that says "Partially Supports" on a criterion and leaves Remarks blank has told them a problem exists and nothing about its size, so the safe reading is the worst one. A report with fewer "Supports" rows but a real sentence on every partial row routinely scores better than a cleaner-looking one that explains nothing.

Which rows actually need remarks?

The ones marked Partially Supports and Does Not Support. Those are the two values a reviewer reads as risk, and Remarks is the only place the document says how much. A Supports row is self-explanatory and a Not Applicable row is usually obvious from the product type, so leaving those blank costs little. The generator on this site flags every Partially Supports or Does Not Support row with empty Remarks before you export.

What header fields do reviewers check first?

Product name, report date, and evaluation methods used. The date tells a reviewer whether the report describes the version being bought or one from three releases ago. Evaluation methods tell them whether the answers came from assistive-technology testing, an automated scan, or somebody's recollection. A report missing either is hard to weigh against a competing vendor's, and those three fields are exactly the ones this generator refuses to let you export quietly.

Is a generic remark better than a blank one?

Only slightly, and WebAIM's procurement guidance names generic remarks as its own failure. "Some issues exist" or "partially conformant" repeated on twelve rows tells a reviewer that the rows were filled in rather than evaluated. A useful remark names what does not work, where, and what a user encounters: which component, which assistive technology, and whether a workaround exists. Two specific sentences beat a paragraph of hedging.

Should we mark a criterion Not Evaluated or guess at it?

Mark it Not Evaluated. It is one of the template's own values and it is the honest label for a row nobody has tested. A guess that turns out wrong is a misrepresentation in a procurement document, which is a far worse position than an admitted gap. A reviewer who sees three Not Evaluated rows with a note about when they will be tested is reading an ACR written by someone who tested the other forty-seven.

How many criteria does an ACR have to cover?

This generator walks the 50 WCAG 2.1 Level A and Level AA success criteria that most ACRs in circulation are scored against, grouped by the four principles in the order the standard and the template both use. It does not cover Level AAA or the nine WCAG 2.2 additions. Check the criterion set against the W3C's own materials and the current ITI template before you submit, the same as every other output of this tool.

Does this tool test our product or choose conformance levels for us?

No, and that limit is deliberate. It never scans, crawls, or assesses anything, and it never selects a level on your behalf. Every conformance value and every remark is yours, entered from your own testing. What it does is format those answers into the standard table shape and flag the completeness problems that get a document sent back. Format and completeness, never assessment.

Is anything we type sent anywhere?

No. The generator runs entirely in your browser tab, with no account and no upload. An optional draft auto-save writes to your own browser's local storage and can be turned off; clearing your browser data clears it. An unreleased product's accessibility gaps are commercially sensitive, which is the reason the tool has no server in the loop at all.
